title: Hank's New Assistant

jokes.text: Your lips look a little cracked. / Of course. They misplaced the lip balm.
jokes.setup: Post-show chaos; someone observes Larry's cracked lips as a minor concern.
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately externalizes blame — 'they misplaced the lip balm' — as if the crew's incompetence is responsible for his body's needs. Classic Larry Sanders narcissism.
jokes.explanation: A small but perfectly Larry joke — he can't just have chapped lips, someone must be at fault. The character integration is high because it establishes his solipsism immediately. Not a showstopper but economical and true to character.

dialogue.line: Your lips look a little cracked.

jokes.text: Excuse me. I hate to be a bother, but is there some religious reason you're not answering my phone?
jokes.setup: Hank's assistant is absent and he needs someone to answer his phone. He approaches what appears to be Larry's assistant.
jokes.punchline: 'Is there some religious reason' — the absurd, passive-aggressive framing of a mundane complaint. Hank performs politeness ('I hate to be a bother') while being maximally rude.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny line. The 'religious reason' framing is unexpected and specific — Hank is so entitled he invents a hypothetical excuse more absurd than the real situation. Strong character integration: only Hank Kingsley phrases an office complaint this way. Economy is excellent — it's one sentence that does a lot of work establishing his pomposity.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Of course. They misplaced the lip balm.

jokes.text: What darlene does is not a job, you see? It's a calling, and I will wait for her return.
jokes.setup: Staff offer to help Hank find a temp for his absent assistant Darlene.
jokes.punchline: Hank elevates being his personal assistant to a near-spiritual vocation, revealing how dependent and delusional he is about the relationship.
jokes.explanation: Deeply character-specific. The word 'calling' positions Hank as someone who genuinely believes he's the center of Darlene's spiritual life. It's funny and a little sad — which is the Larry Sanders sweet spot. Sets up the devastating irony of the Darlene letter later.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Excuse me. I hate to be a bother, but is there some religious reason you're not answering my phone?

jokes.text: Hey, look out, me boy, I found me lucky poker hat.
jokes.setup: Artie appears wearing a hat, cheerfully announcing poker plans.
jokes.punchline: The 'lucky poker hat' bit is funny as a character detail — Artie having a dedicated poker hat is absurdly specific — but the real punchline is that the tape Larry wanted to hide is under the hat, which Artie then reveals.
jokes.explanation: The hat-hiding-the-tape is a nice structural setup that pays off immediately. Artie's folksy bluster ('me lucky poker hat') contrasts with his mischievous awareness. Functions as both a visual gag and character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: What darlene does is not a job, you see? It's a calling, and I will wait for her return.

jokes.text: Larry discovers the Dana Carvey tape is under Artie's hat — Artie had been hiding it from him.
jokes.setup: Larry asks Artie about the tape of Carvey's SNL impression of him. Artie says he doesn't know anything.
jokes.punchline: Larry notices the tape is literally under the hat Artie is wearing. Artie cheerfully reveals it: 'Oh! Ho ho ho.' He knew all along.
jokes.explanation: Elegant physical comedy embedded in dialogue. 'Oh! Ho ho ho' is Rip Torn at his best — the gleeful guilty laugh of someone who's been caught being mischievous on purpose. Structurally clean setup and reveal. The rewatch bonus is high because knowing Artie hid it deliberately reframes the whole opening beat.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Hey, look out, me boy, I found me lucky poker hat.

jokes.text: I wouldn't do that. / Yeah. I want to see it. / You'll love it.
jokes.setup: Larry says he wants to watch the Carvey impression tape. Artie warns him off.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'You'll love it' — delivered with knowing irony — signals that Larry absolutely will not love it. The gap between the warm words and the dry delivery is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Clean deadpan from Artie, economical. Works as setup for the tape-watching sequence rather than as a standalone joke. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Wayne's world money!

jokes.text: Just remember that all America loves you.
jokes.setup: Larry is about to watch a mocking impression of himself on national television.
jokes.punchline: Artie's reassurance is perfectly calibrated — it's both true (Larry IS beloved) and completely beside the point (that won't stop the impression from stinging). Delivered deadpan right before the pain begins.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical. Seven words that capture the Artie-Larry dynamic perfectly — Artie as fixer, enabler, and knowing witness to Larry's vanity. The humor is in the gentle futility of the reassurance. High economy score because every word is load-bearing.

jokes.text: Larry watching the Carvey impression and growing increasingly agitated while Artie stands in front of the TV blocking his view.
jokes.setup: Larry sits down to watch the tape. Artie apparently positions himself in front of the TV.
jokes.punchline: Larry: 'W... I can't... what are you doing? I can't see.' Artie: 'I'm shoving it up.' The physical comedy of Artie literally obstructing Larry's view — possibly deliberately — while Larry squirms is visual cringe.
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that works better in vision than in transcript. The 'I'm shoving it up' line is odd and the moment relies heavily on Rip Torn's physical presence. Functional but not the sharpest beat in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I think he's on crack.

jokes.text: Are you working out or something? You're getting very wide.
jokes.setup: Artie is blocking the TV. Larry needs him to move.
jokes.punchline: Instead of just asking Artie to move, Larry makes it an insult about Artie's size — which is itself a deflection from his anxiety about the tape. Pure passive aggression disguised as casual observation.
jokes.explanation: Nice character beat — Larry's anxiety manifests as a dig at Artie. Works within the scene but not a standalone gem.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You're getting very wide.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'm shoving it up.

jokes.text: Yasir Arafat, the first terrorist nominated for the peace prize. This is sort of akin to Madonna being nominated for best virgin.
characters: Dana Carvey (as Larry Sanders on TV)
jokes.setup: The Carvey impression plays on TV — he's doing Larry's monologue style with topical jokes.
jokes.punchline: The Madonna/virgin comparison is the punchline. It's a functional topical joke of the era — the structure is solid (terrorist/peace :: Madonna/virgin) — but the humor comes as much from watching Larry react as from the joke itself.
jokes.explanation: The joke-within-a-show functions as a period-accurate late-night monologue gag. The structure (A:B :: C:D analogy) is sound but the material is generic mid-90s topical comedy. Its real function is to give Larry something to react to — the reaction is funnier than the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Chinless little cocksuckers.

jokes.text: Well, it's not... accurate at all. / Of course not. It's just more of that shit they do on Saturday Night Live.
jokes.setup: Larry watches Carvey do his monologue impression and complains it's inaccurate.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Of course not' — validating Larry while dismissing SNL wholesale — is both sycophantic and genuine. The comedy is in Artie's practiced talent for managing Larry's ego.
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy — Artie as Larry's professional ego-cushion is a recurring dynamic and this is a clean instance of it.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, you... you lilt.

jokes.text: My chin doesn't look like that, does it? / You have a beautiful chin. All those people on Saturday Night Live, they just wish they had a chin like yours. Chinless little cocksuckers.
jokes.setup: Larry frets that Carvey's impression makes his chin look strange. He asks Artie if his chin looks like that.
jokes.punchline: Artie's escalation from 'You have a beautiful chin' (gentle reassurance) to 'Chinless little cocksuckers' (nuclear rage) in one breath is the joke. The absurd intensity of Artie's loyalty.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalation from tender compliment to vicious epithet in one sentence is perfectly constructed. It's deeply character-specific — only Artie could weaponize affection this way. 'Chinless little cocksuckers' is quotable, shocking, and earned because we've watched Artie position himself as Larry's protector. The structure (reassurance → attack) follows a classic escalation pattern executed with unusual ferocity. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor: sharp, unexpected, perfectly economical.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Fuck you.

jokes.text: Why is he whining like that? I mean, I don't whine like that. / No, not like that. / What do you mean, not like that? / Well, you... you lilt.
jokes.setup: Larry objects that the impression makes him look like he whines.
jokes.punchline: Artie, trying to reassure him, says 'No, not like that' — then is forced to clarify. 'You lilt' is the punchline: a diplomatic word that confirms the underlying complaint while technically denying it. Larry whines; Artie just calls it something prettier.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's standout joke. The four-line exchange is a masterpiece of cringe comedy construction. Larry walks into the trap himself — pressing Artie for a denial he can't give. 'You lilt' is a perfect word: polite, precise, and absolutely devastating. It confirms everything the impression showed while being technically a compliment. Maximum funny-per-word, could only exist between these two characters, and the structure (denial → qualification → exposure) is pristine. Comfortably in the 8+ tier.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'm tracing this call right now! Pound sand up your ass.

jokes.text: He wants to do this on the show. Are you aware of that? / I don't know why he thinks it's funny. He looks like Tim Curry.
jokes.setup: Larry reveals Carvey wants to do the impression live on the show.
jokes.punchline: 'He looks like Tim Curry' — Larry's deflection. He can't admit it's an accurate impression of him, so he attacks the impression itself by noting Carvey looks like someone else entirely. The non sequitur logic is very Larry.
jokes.explanation: Solid character laugh. 'He looks like Tim Curry' is a specific, unexpected insult that reveals Larry's wounded vanity. The illogic (Carvey's looks are irrelevant to whether the impression is accurate) is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: From the cirque du soleil. The sad clown, right?

jokes.text: Don't tell him no. Then it'll look like I can't laugh at myself, and we know that's not true.
jokes.setup: Artie suggests just telling Carvey he can't do the impression. Larry overrules him.
jokes.punchline: Larry insists on telling Carvey to go ahead — entirely to protect his image of being a good sport. 'We know that's not true' — delivered straight, meant sincerely, but the entire episode has already shown it IS true. Beautiful dramatic irony.
jokes.explanation: The irony is rich and structural — the whole episode pivots on this line. Larry's complete lack of self-awareness delivered with absolute confidence. 'We know that's not true' is the funniest kind of wrong statement: the speaker believes it completely. Strong character integration because it's a sentence that could only come from Larry Sanders.

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: Remember? Everybody put on their protective goggles, and let's all play double danger. Double danger.

jokes.text: That's why you, sir, are the greatest man in show business.
jokes.setup: After Larry decides to let Carvey do the impression (for entirely self-serving, image-protecting reasons), Artie praises him.
jokes.punchline: Artie's grandiose flattery is both sincere and absurd. The humor is in how effortlessly Artie administers the ego stroke and how readily Larry accepts it.
jokes.explanation: Functional Artie-Larry dynamic joke. Works as a beat but follows naturally from joke #15 without adding much new.

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: Well, actually, I was the personal assistant to her personal assistant.

jokes.text: Hello? / ... / Fuck you.
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to answer phones because his assistant is absent.
jokes.punchline: Hank's exasperated 'Fuck you' to the phone — after presumably getting a bad connection or silence — delivered as a professional response.
jokes.explanation: The timing of this is everything. Hank says 'Hello?' into the phone with professional affect, and then without transition says 'Fuck you.' The gap between the greeting and the expletive is pure character comedy. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: She made him clean the hair out of her tub.

jokes.text: Hello? / ... / I'm tracing this call right now! / Pound sand up your ass.
jokes.setup: Hank continues answering phones badly. Another frustrating call.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'I'm tracing this call right now!' (absurd bluster) to 'Pound sand up your ass' (graphic folksy insult) is a running gag on Hank's phone incompetence.
jokes.explanation: 'Pound sand up your ass' is a wonderfully specific, old-fashioned insult that sounds like something Hank would have learned from a 1970s variety show. The threat to trace the call is perfect Hank bluster. Running gag escalates nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: Oh, our nation's capital.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Canada.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I know!

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Canada.

jokes.text: Delete? What... what is delete?
jokes.setup: Hank apparently encounters the office computer/voicemail system.
jokes.punchline: Hank's confusion with basic technology — 'What is delete?' — establishes him as hilariously out of touch.
jokes.explanation: Competent character laugh — Hank as technological dinosaur. Functional but not particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Don't speak to Larry unless he speaks to you.

jokes.text: Oh. / Oh, of course. / From the cirque du soleil. / The sad clown, right? / No, no. You're thinking of Pinno. / This is Brian.
jokes.setup: A staff member introduces a friend who needs a job as Hank's temporary assistant. Brian apparently has an unusual appearance.
jokes.punchline: Hank immediately recognizes Brian (or thinks he does) as 'the sad clown from Cirque du Soleil.' He's either wrong or this is his version of a compliment. 'You're thinking of Pinno' — a specific fake name for a Cirque performer — makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist beat. Hank's confident misidentification is very Hank, and 'You're thinking of Pinno' is a brilliantly specific straight-man correction to an insane premise. The specificity of a fake Cirque performer's name elevates it.

dialogue.line: Fat lips.

jokes.text: I've been a big fan ever since you hosted Double Danger. Remember? Everybody put on their protective goggles, and let's all play Double Danger.
jokes.setup: Brian says he's a big fan of Hank's and mentions a specific show as evidence.
jokes.punchline: 'Double Danger' — an obscure, clearly terrible game show where audience members needed protective goggles — is the joke. The specificity of the safety goggles is perfect. Hank is flattered.
jokes.explanation: An excellent industry-insider joke. 'Double Danger' is clearly a D-tier game show that only the most dedicated Hank fan would know — which makes it simultaneously touching (Brian really IS a fan) and pathetic (this is what Hank's legacy consists of). The protective goggles detail is inspired specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: I've earned the right to leave the room.

jokes.text: Wow! Personal assistant to Barbara Streisand? / Well, actually, I was the personal assistant to her personal assistant.
jokes.setup: Hank reads Brian's resume and is impressed by the Streisand connection.
jokes.punchline: The assistant-to-the-assistant reveal deflates the prestige instantly. The hierarchy of Hollywood assistants as its own absurd ecosystem.
jokes.explanation: Classic Hollywood satire. The sub-assistant status is a perfect industry-specific joke about how many layers of gatekeeping exist around celebrity. Clean setup-punchline structure with good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hard-on cream? No, I forgot it.

jokes.text: And, uh, you left that job because... / Well, I really can't say because I signed the confidentiality agreement. / She made him clean the hair out of her tub.
jokes.setup: Hank asks why Brian left Streisand's employ. Brian says he can't say due to an NDA.
jokes.punchline: A third party immediately blurts the secret anyway: 'She made him clean the hair out of her tub.' The grotesque specificity of the Streisand hair-in-the-tub detail, combined with the NDA being instantly violated, is perfectly constructed.
jokes.explanation: Excellent construction. Three moving parts: (1) the important-sounding NDA, (2) Brian's dignified silence, (3) the anticlimactic yet specific violation — tub hair. The joke works because 'cleaning hair from a celebrity's tub' is both believably humiliating and grotesquely specific. It's also a sly dig at Streisand's diva reputation. The third-party immediate leak makes it a meta-joke about Hollywood confidentiality. Justifiably scores 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I could never talk this way around darlene. She'd just get all insulted.

jokes.text: Paula, the woman wears a lot of hats.
jokes.setup: Paula reveals Streisand made Brian clean her tub hair. Brian tries to dignify the situation.
jokes.punchline: Hank defends Streisand by saying 'the woman wears a lot of hats' — the idiom meaning she does many things, but also potentially a literal reference to the wigs/headpieces Streisand is famous for. Double meaning, possibly unintentional by Hank.
jokes.explanation: Solid quick joke. The idiom lands well whether or not the hat/wig double meaning is intentional — either way Hank's defense of a celebrity who made her sub-assistant clean tub hair is absurdly misplaced loyalty.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'll be in my office whacking off.

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: Okay. Uh, I'll hold all your calls.

jokes.text: Oh, our nation's capital. / Canada. / I know! Canada. / Close.
jokes.setup: Brian says he's from British Columbia. Hank identifies it as 'our nation's capital.'
jokes.punchline: 'Canada. / I know! Canada.' — Hank doesn't know that British Columbia is Canadian, or confuses it with Washington D.C. When corrected, his 'I know! Canada' followed by 'Close' from someone is perfectly absurd. He knew and didn't know simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: Efficient and funny. Hank's geography stupidity is established in three lines and the 'I know! Canada. / Close.' exchange has a lovely rhythm. 'Close' is doing a lot of work — it's both an absurd consolation (Canada is not close to being America's capital) and delivered deadpan. Strong character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: The Chinese call it a feng shui, the placement of objects in a room to maximize your harmony and power.

jokes.text: Please, you got the job. Help me.
jokes.setup: The job interview has gone on too long with Hank suffering without an assistant.
jokes.punchline: Hank abandons any further pretense of evaluation — his desperation ('Help me') is the punchline. The formalities of hiring collapse into naked need.
jokes.explanation: Four words that are perfectly Hank. 'Help me' stripped of any professional veneer. The economy is outstanding — this line encapsulates Hank's dependency, his desperation about Darlene, and his fundamental inability to function independently. Very quotable.

dialogue.line: Has she lost any weight?

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: No!

jokes.text: Fred Travalina. / Um, he can't be reached right now. He's in a meeting. May I take a message?
jokes.setup: Brian immediately gets on the phone and handles a call for Hank — perfectly, professionally.
jokes.punchline: The contrast between Hank's catastrophic phone handling moments earlier ('Fuck you,' 'Pound sand up your ass') and Brian's instant competence is the joke. Brian shows in five seconds what Hank couldn't manage in five minutes.
jokes.explanation: The callback structure is elegant. Brian doesn't need to prove himself — just answering the phone normally is an implicit rebuke to everything we just watched Hank do. The Travalina name-drop (a real but obscure impressionist) is a nice insider touch.

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: You know, the toughest people are the ones who can cry.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'm tough.

jokes.text: Little tip... don't speak to Larry unless he speaks to you.
jokes.setup: Artie welcomes Brian to 'the family' and immediately gives him survival advice.
jokes.punchline: The tip — don't speak to Larry unless spoken to — frames the star of the show as a potentate who must not be addressed directly. Delivered warmly ('Have fun, my boy') which makes the feudal dynamic even funnier.
jokes.explanation: Sharp industry-world-building joke. The fact that a talk show host requires such court-like protocols is both satirically pointed and funny. Artie's delivery ('Nice suit. / Have fun, my boy.') combined with this warning creates a tonal whiplash that's very Larry Sanders.

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: Hey, life, take your best shot, 'cause to Mr. Hank Kingsley, life is a carousel, and the sun is a scoop of ice cream.

jokes.text: Are my lips that fat? / No, Larry, they're not. / Really? / You know what the kids used to call me when I was little? / No. / Fat lips.
jokes.setup: Larry is watching the Carvey impression and spiraling into self-examination. He asks about his lips.
jokes.punchline: Larry's childhood nickname 'Fat Lips' — volunteered unprompted and with total sincerity — is a perfectly calibrated moment of Larry Sanders neurotic oversharing. The specificity (fat lips as a childhood trauma) elevates it above generic vanity comedy.
jokes.explanation: The structural delivery — the long pause implied before 'Fat lips' — is excellent. Larry leading someone through a whole preamble ('You know what the kids used to call me?') to reveal a childhood nickname that he's still haunted by is perfect character comedy. Only Larry Sanders would volunteer this in a professional context.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Are you gay?

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: Yeah, but that was two years ago, and I got over it.

jokes.text: At least they're not out of proportion with your teeth. / You know what the kids used to call my teeth when I was little? / You know what? I can't do this anymore, Larry.
jokes.setup: The reassurer tries to pivot away from lips by noting Larry's teeth are fine.
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately pivots to teeth — revealing a SECOND childhood nickname spiral incoming. The reassurer cuts him off in exhaustion before he can get there. The joke is the promise of an even worse nickname and the other person's absolute refusal to hear it.
jokes.explanation: The escalation here is excellent — the setup from joke #30 (fat lips nickname) leads us to anticipate an equally humiliating teeth nickname, but we never hear it. The comedic payoff IS the refusal to continue. 'You know what? I can't do this anymore, Larry' breaks the fourth wall of the conversation in a way that's very proto-Office. Strong structure: setup, callback, escalation, subverted punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It's Steve. Steve. God damn it!

jokes.text: I already told you that your butt, your lips, and your teeth are all fine. / No... okay. So it's my chin. That's what it is.
jokes.setup: The exasperated reassurer lists everything they've already cleared: butt, lips, teeth.
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately pivots to a new body part — his chin — as if the other three were solved problems and chin is the real issue. The list of anatomical insecurities is the running gag of the sequence.
jokes.explanation: The cataloguing of body parts — butt, lips, teeth — reveals the scope of Larry's body dysmorphia and is funny as a list. His pivot to chin as 'the real issue' is perfectly timed escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, that's 'cause it's 50 cents now. It just went up a couple years ago. You wouldn't have known that.

jokes.text: You know, I've earned the right to leave the room.
jokes.setup: Larry continues his body-part neurosis spiral despite repeated reassurances.
jokes.punchline: The formal invocation of 'I've earned the right' — as though leaving a conversation requires earned credentials — is the joke. It's an absurdly legalistic way to say 'I'm done talking to you.'
jokes.explanation: Quotable and economical. 'I've earned the right to leave the room' is a line that could be lifted from this episode and used in daily life. Its humor comes from the implication that leaving a narcissist's spiral requires formal entitlement. Very strong economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: He's gay? Well, don't tell Dana carvey, 'cause you know what? He'll do an impression of him.

jokes.text: Mouthwash? Mm-hmm. Eye drops? Odor-eaters? Size 12 for the big man. Mm-hmm. Hand lotion? Check. All right. Hard-on cream? / No, I forgot it.
jokes.setup: Brian is delivering Hank's personal supplies, going through a checklist that sounds like a standard self-care kit.
jokes.punchline: 'Hard-on cream?' — the checklist escalates from mundane grooming items to an erectile product, which Brian simply forgot. Hank's total comfort with asking and Brian's casual 'I forgot it' reply treat it as unremarkable.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke construction. The checklist format is a classic setup — each mundane item lowers the audience's guard slightly more before the escalation to 'hard-on cream.' What makes it exceptional is that neither character treats this as remarkable. The normalization of the absurd is very Larry Sanders. Brian's flat 'No, I forgot it' is a perfect straight-line punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: A gay? What are you? Italian?

jokes.text: Okay. I'll be in my office whacking off. / Okay. Uh, I'll hold all your calls.
jokes.setup: Hank wraps up the supply delivery and announces his plans.
jokes.punchline: Hank announces he's going to masturbate in his office with the casual affect of saying 'I'll be in a meeting.' Brian's 'I'll hold all your calls' treats this as equally routine office procedure.
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly economical. The joke is entirely in the register mismatch: Hank's deadpan announcement of masturbation as a professional activity, and Brian's immediate professional response treating it as such. No buildup needed — the punchline IS the normality. The 'hold all my calls' callback structure makes it a tiny perfect scene. High quotability because it's usable as an out-of-context line.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Maybe this will be your first chance to fuck your assistant.

jokes.text: Brian! / Coming! Coming!
jokes.setup: Hank calls for Brian from his office — immediately after announcing he's going to masturbate.
jokes.punchline: Brian yells 'Coming! Coming!' — the innocent meaning is 'I'm on my way,' but the double entendre given the previous announcement is the laugh. The timing (immediate, from Brian's breathless running) sells it.
jokes.explanation: The double entendre is set up beautifully by the previous beat. It's not sophisticated wordplay, but the timing and economy make it work. Earns its impact score from the callback context.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: There was not one indication on that resume that he was gay. Not... not... not one.

jokes.text: I love this. You do? / What... what did you do? I mean, the room, it just seems... I don't know. It's so much bigger. / Yeah. The Chinese call it a feng shui... to maximize your harmony and power. / Ah. Well, since my divorce, my dick could use a little feng shui.
jokes.setup: Brian has rearranged Hank's office using feng shui principles. Hank is delighted by how much bigger the room feels.
jokes.punchline: 'Since my divorce, my dick could use a little feng shui.' Hank maps the concept of 'harmony and power' directly onto his genitals with a logic that is both absurd and perfectly Hank.
jokes.explanation: Good joke that earns its punchline. 'My dick could use a little feng shui' is a memorable, quotable line that works because the logic is almost coherent — feng shui IS about harmony and power flow, and Hank post-divorce desperately needs both. Character-integrated because it's simultaneously crude and kind of earnest. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Barbara streisand. Aw. Aw, shit.

jokes.text: Hank reads the Darlene letter aloud to gathered staff: 'I have met a wonderful man, a holy man. He lives in India, and I have decided to follow him. He has shown me the true way, and I have been reborn into truth and light. And I now know that I can never return to the life that I had there with all of you.'
jokes.setup: Hank announces to the assembled staff that Darlene has written. He reads the letter triumphantly.
jokes.punchline: The letter is a goodbye — Darlene has joined a cult-adjacent spiritual movement in India and is never coming back. The absurdity escalates through: the holy man, following him to India, being 'reborn into truth and light,' and the definitive abandonment. Hank's public performance of this letter as a joyful event before it turns on him is the cringe structure.
jokes.explanation: This is a sustained cringe-comedy crescendo. The setup from joke #3 (Darlene's job is a 'calling,' he'll wait for her return) pays off devastatingly: the one who felt 'called' was Darlene, just not to Hank. The public reading amplifies the humiliation. Staff reactions mid-letter ('Hello, Beverly.' 'Fine, Darlene.' 'No!') are perfectly timed interruptions that both humanize the staff and delay the devastating final paragraph. Excellent structure.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yes, I asked for lanolin. I asked for lanolin. Darlene was with me for six years. She never did this.

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: Hank, you asked for aloe vera.

jokes.text: Please say hello to her for me. / Hello, Beverly. / How is Paula? / Fine, Darlene. / Has she lost any weight? / No! / I love her more than she can love herself.
jokes.setup: The staff responds to Darlene's letter being read aloud as if she's present in the room — answering her questions in real time.
jokes.punchline: Paula's 'No!' to 'has she lost any weight?' is the best reaction — the raw, immediate self-consciousness of the response, followed by Darlene's pre-written 'I love her more than she can love herself.' The letter's affection lands as a backhanded compliment.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional scene construction. The staff treating Darlene's letter as a two-way conversation is absurdly sweet, and the weight question/Paula reaction is a perfect embedded joke. 'I love her more than she can love herself' is a pitch-perfect line for a cult-follower's letter — it sounds profound and is kind of insulting simultaneously. The juxtaposition of real-time office banter against a goodbye letter is deeply funny and a little heartbreaking.

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: So this has nothing to do with me being gay, does it?

jokes.text: Hank begins breaking down while reading the final section of the Darlene letter, then falls silent for 17 seconds.
jokes.setup: Hank has been performing the letter-reading confidently. The final paragraph — 'Please forgive me, Hank. I'll miss...' — stops him.
jokes.punchline: The 17-second silence. The comedy is in the public nature of Hank's grief — he assembled the staff for what he thought would be a triumphant reading — and the yawning gap where words should be.
jokes.explanation: This is the finest pure-comedy-through-silence moment in the episode. The 17-second gap is not funny in isolation — it's devastating — but the setup (Hank's pompous public ceremony, the staff assembled, his confidence) makes it a masterclass in cringe comedy. The economy score approaches maximum because zero words are spoken and yet everything is communicated. Only Jeffrey Tambor playing Hank Kingsley in this specific moment with this specific backstory could make this land. Quotability is near-zero (you can't quote silence), but the impact is among the highest in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I wore a red ribbon to the emmys. I have been to several elton John concerts.

jokes.text: This is sort of akin to Madonna being nominated for best virgin.
characters: Larry (on-air, visible through monitor or remembered)
jokes.setup: Following Hank's breakdown over the letter, we cut or hear a snippet of Larry's monologue — the same joke from the Carvey impression tape.
jokes.punchline: The same joke appears twice — first as Carvey's impression on the tape Larry was sensitive about, now as background dressing. The repetition creates a commentary on the late-night machine's indifference to personal crisis.
jokes.explanation: The structural decision to replay the same joke from the tape — right after Hank's private devastation — is a Larry Sanders Show signature move. The show continues. Life goes on. The repetition is not just callback; it's ironic commentary.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I mean, look at my ass. I'm touching my ass.

jokes.text: Larry tells a staffer he has 'an appointment with the Swedish bikini team' and gets interrupted by Dana Carvey's arrival announcement mid-absurd-statement
jokes.setup: Larry is in his office doing something; Carvey's arrival is announced
jokes.punchline: Larry's mid-sentence 'appointment with the Swedish bikini team' is an obvious deflection/fantasy that gets cut off — the comedy is the banality of the interruption meeting the grandiosity of the excuse
jokes.explanation: A throwaway gag. 'Swedish bikini team' is a dated 1990s reference deployed here as a generic celebrity-braggart excuse. Not very original and doesn't add much character texture beyond 'Larry tries to seem cool.' Functional filler.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.line: You said versace, and you touched yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I touched myself on the leg.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.line: Why does yourself have to mean penis?

jokes.text: Darlene would never let me smoke. / No? Mm-mm.
jokes.setup: Hank is smoking after the emotional Darlene letter revelation. He reflects on Darlene's rules.
jokes.punchline: The simple observation that Darlene controlled whether he smoked — delivered quietly, post-breakdown — reveals the depth and specificity of their relationship. The comedy is in the mundane detail against the emotional backdrop.
jokes.explanation: Quiet, effective character moment. The specificity of the smoking prohibition reveals the maternal aspect of Darlene's role in Hank's life — she managed not just his schedule but his vices. Works emotionally and comedically.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.line: People say I flip-flop, and I don't. But then again, I do.

jokes.text: You know, the toughest people are the ones who can cry. / I'm tough. / Yeah, you are. / You're tough, sir. / Hey, life, take your best shot, 'cause to Mr. Hank Kingsley, life is a carousel, and the sun is a scoop of ice cream. Yeah, so blow away those clouds that rain on his parade.
jokes.setup: Brian is consoling the weeping Hank after the Darlene letter.
jokes.punchline: Brian's pep talk escalates into a bizarre extended metaphor: life as carousel, sun as ice cream, clouds raining on his parade — delivered with increasing theatrical intensity. It's simultaneously sincere and completely insane.
jokes.explanation: Brian's pep talk is written in deliberately mixed metaphors — carousel, ice cream, rainy parade — that individually are greeting-card sentiments but together become absurdist noise. The joke is that Hank finds this genuinely comforting. It establishes Brian as someone with more heart than sense, which will make his firing more poignant.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.line: Why should I be mad? I have many arrows in my comedic arsenal, Larry. Let's put the Larry Sanders arrow back in the sheath and pull out the Jimmy Stewart arrow. Bing. Bull's-eye!

jokes.text: Oh, they didn't mention that to me. / No, we're going to do it. / I'm going to get the teeth, the whole thing, we'll do it back and forth like I used to do with Dennis Miller. / It always killed. Remember that?
jokes.setup: Larry tells Carvey the impression is going ahead. Carvey mentions he wasn't told this.
jokes.punchline: Larry's breezy 'It always killed' about the Dennis Miller bits — delivered with absolute confidence about something Carvey can neither confirm nor deny — is pure Larry. He's selling himself to the guest on his own show.
jokes.explanation: Functional industry-comedy beat. Larry's casual assumption that famous people remember his bits is very on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'd take that little Dana carvey and I'd dry-shave him with a flicker.

jokes.text: Carvey, I don't want to be ca-kwee-cas here, but I feel squeaky in my squawker. Buck-buck. I'm like aweecabah.
jokes.setup: Larry is attempting a bit with Carvey, apparently doing some kind of voice or impression.
jokes.punchline: The gibberish — 'ca-kwee-cas,' 'squeaky in my squawker,' 'aweecabah' — seems to be Larry doing a bad impression of something, possibly Carvey's style or a character. The comedy is in its complete incoherence and Larry's evident satisfaction with it.
jokes.explanation: The humor here is in Larry's performance of being a performer — the gibberish is the joke about Larry's comedic pretensions. Works as a character beat more than as a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I am, but where else am I going to find a personal assistant who'll tell me when Larry is hurt?

jokes.text: You are so tense. Give it up. There you go. / Oh, that's good. / You can feel it. I can tell. I can feel it all in your back. You're mad. You're angry because Darlene ran away, right? 'Cause she left you.
jokes.setup: Carvey begins giving Larry a back massage during what should be a professional green-room conversation.
jokes.punchline: Carvey's impromptu massage followed by amateur psychoanalysis — 'You're angry because Darlene ran away' — turns a celebrity green-room chat into an encounter therapy session. The inappropriateness is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The Carvey-as-unlicensed-therapist bit is amusing but the scene runs slightly long. The cringe comes from the inappropriate intimacy of a celebrity guest giving another celebrity a back massage while making confident psychological assessments.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Doug llewelyn's a faggot. Sorry.

jokes.text: I know. I felt exactly the same way when Keith ran off. / I'm sorry. Who's Keith? Your dog? / No, he was my lover. We were together for five years.
jokes.setup: Brian is consoling Hank about Darlene by sharing his own experience of abandonment.
jokes.punchline: Hank assumes Keith is a dog. Brian clarifies Keith was his lover — male — and they were together five years. The misdirection (dog → gay lover) combined with the casual delivery is the punchline. Hank's confusion follows.
jokes.explanation: The 'Your dog?' misdirection is perfectly timed. Hank's charitable assumption (lost a pet) vs. the reality (gay relationship) is structurally clean. The five-year detail makes it a real comparison to Darlene's six-year tenure, which adds weight. The moment Hank realizes is the beginning of a prolonged cringe sequence — this beat is the trigger for the episode's best sustained comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: I worked on a Cruise ship for eight years. I did nothing but play poker. I am going to kick their asses.

jokes.text: Sorry, um, I'm not... I'm not following you. You... your lover? / Yeah, he was my boyfriend. / Mmm. Yeah. / Are you... um... are you gay? / Yeah, but that was two years ago, and I got over it. / So, you're not... you're not gay. / What do you mean?
jokes.setup: Brian has revealed Keith was his male lover. Hank is processing this in real time.
jokes.punchline: Brian says 'Yeah, but that was two years ago, and I got over it' — as if being gay is something you recover from, like a cold. Hank, desperate for this to make sense, pounces: 'So you're not gay.' Brian's genuine confusion at Hank's interpretation ('What do you mean?') is the escalation.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding. 'Yeah, but that was two years ago, and I got over it' is a line that operates on multiple levels simultaneously: Brian seems to think 'getting over' Keith (the breakup) answers the question about being gay; Hank desperately interprets it as Brian having 'gotten over' homosexuality entirely. The collision between what each character means is pure Larry Sanders Show gold. Deeply quotable, character-specific to Brian's particular idiolect, and the structure of the misunderstanding is airtight. Comfortably 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, I got a boner.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Whoa, we're all in trouble.

jokes.text: His chin is all puffed out, you know, and I don't think that I look like that. / I wouldn't know, Mr. Sanders. I haven't seen that show since Eddie Murphy left. / Yeah, well, I can understand that.
jokes.setup: Larry is venting about the Carvey impression to someone (apparently a parking attendant or similar). The listener admits they don't watch SNL.
jokes.punchline: 'I haven't seen that show since Eddie Murphy left.' Eddie Murphy left SNL in 1984 — a decade before this episode. The line both dismisses SNL as unwatchable post-Murphy AND establishes that this person hasn't watched the show in ten years, making them comically useless as a reference point. Larry: 'Yeah, well, I can understand that.' — complete agreement.
jokes.explanation: Good industry joke. The Eddie Murphy departure as the endpoint of SNL's watchability is a specific, era-accurate pop culture reference that works as both comedy and commentary. Larry's immediate validation ('Yeah, well, I can understand that') shows how much he wants anyone to agree with his negative view of the show.

jokes.text: He walks around whining, and he's always rubbing his ass, and he goes, 'Oh, my... does my ass look fat? Does my ass look fat?' / I don't think I do that, do I?
jokes.setup: Larry is describing the Carvey impression to someone, demonstrating what Carvey does.
jokes.punchline: Larry acts out the impression ('does my ass look fat?') while literally performing the behavior (asking self-consciously about his appearance) to someone who doesn't know him. The recursion — Larry doing an impression of Carvey doing Larry, while doing exactly what Larry does — is perfect.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's structurally best jokes. Larry is performing the Carvey impression to prove how unfair it is — while simultaneously doing exactly what the impression mocks. 'Does my ass look fat?' immediately followed by 'I don't think I do that, do I?' IS the impression in real life. The self-undermining is perfectly constructed and character-essential. Only Larry Sanders could be this perfectly unself-aware.

jokes.text: I got to run. My truck's parked in a red zone. / All right. Okay. Well, good to talk to you, Sam. / It's Steve. Steve. / God damn it!
jokes.setup: Larry has been venting to someone (a parking attendant or similar) about the Carvey impression.
jokes.punchline: Larry calls him 'Sam.' His name is Steve. Larry doesn't know the name of the person he just spent several minutes with. The 'God damn it!' — presumably at himself — is both self-aware and funny because it implies this happens all the time.
jokes.explanation: Clean character joke. Larry's inability to remember the name of someone he just had an intimate conversation with is very Larry Sanders — the incidental people in his life are props. 'God damn it!' shows he knows this is a flaw he can't fix.

jokes.text: Hank, what are you doing? / I put a quarter in, and then nothing came out. / Well, that's 'cause it's 50 cents now. It just went up a couple years ago. / You wouldn't have known that. / Well, thank you. I wanted... coke. / Oh. That's fine. Juice is great. Thanks.
jokes.setup: Hank is struggling with a vending machine.
jokes.punchline: Hank's gracious acceptance of juice when he wanted Coke — 'Oh. That's fine. Juice is great. Thanks.' — after Artie explains the price change. The resigned dignity of a man defeated by a vending machine is very Hank.
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat. Hank's helplessness with basic technology (vending machine, phone, computer earlier) is a running thread. The politeness with which he accepts the wrong outcome is touching and funny.

jokes.text: Now, see, Neil Simon, he whines. Why doesn't Dana Carvey do an impression of Neil Simon?
jokes.setup: Artie tells Larry that Neil Simon dropped out of the poker game.
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately repurposes the information as an argument against the Carvey impression — 'Neil Simon whines, do him instead!' — which both reveals Larry's ongoing fixation with the impression and is a funny industry-insider insult to Simon.
jokes.explanation: Nice character beat. Larry can't stop thinking about the impression; everything gets filtered through it. The Neil Simon aside is a funny industry dig.

jokes.text: Oh, great, you guys playing poker? I'll come. / I'm sorry. We just gave that invitation to Barry Levinson.
jokes.setup: Carvey casually invites himself to the poker game.
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately, smoothly, completely invents the excuse that Barry Levinson just got the slot. The instant fabrication — delivered without a beat — is both a rebuff and an industry joke (Barry Levinson as a poker game participant is a specific Hollywood name to drop).
jokes.explanation: Excellent Artie beat. The specificity of 'Barry Levinson' as the fake excuse — a real director, random enough that Carvey can't dispute it — is perfectly chosen. Artie's ability to manufacture a Hollywood excuse at zero notice is a great character detail. Economy is outstanding.

jokes.text: He's gay! / He's gay? / Well, don't tell Dana Carvey, 'cause you know what? He'll do an impression of him.
jokes.setup: Hank reveals to Artie that Brian is gay. He's clearly agitated about this.
jokes.punchline: Artie's response — 'Don't tell Dana Carvey, he'll do an impression of him' — is a callback to the episode's Carvey impression thread while also being a wry comment on Carvey's whole impressionist persona. The logic is absurd but internally consistent.
jokes.explanation: Sharp callback that earns its 8+ score. 'Don't tell Dana Carvey, he'll do an impression of him' is a great line: it's absurd (Carvey doesn't do impressions of random gay guys), it escalates the Carvey impression paranoia, and it perfectly captures Artie's ability to deflate tension with an unexpected comic pivot. The line lands because it's surprising, yet internally logical to the episode's world. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: How would you feel if Beverly was a gay? / A gay? What are you? Italian?
jokes.setup: Hank tries to make Artie understand his discomfort by using a hypothetical about Beverly.
jokes.punchline: 'A gay' — using the indefinite article with a categorical noun — is a malapropism/regionalism that Artie immediately mocks: 'What are you? Italian?' The joke is on the linguistic construction as a marker of Hank's specific cultural background or ignorance.
jokes.explanation: Wonderful quick joke. 'A gay' as a noun construction, and Artie's immediate ethnic-grammar joke, is very fast and very funny. The wordplay is on the article 'a' turning an adjective into a category noun — a specific linguistic tic that Artie clocks immediately. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Maybe this will be your first chance to fuck your assistant.
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to find a silver lining in Hank having a gay male assistant.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'bright side' is that Hank can now sexually pursue his assistant — which would have been wrong with female Darlene but is... also wrong with Brian. The logic is completely inverted and delivered as genuine counsel.
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn delivering this as earnest advice is perfectly Artie. The line is dark (implying he thinks this is a legitimate option) and character-specific (only Artie gives this kind of counsel). The subversion is that his 'bright side' is only slightly less inappropriate than Hank's actual concerns.

jokes.text: There was not one indication on that resume that he was gay. Not... not... not one.
jokes.setup: Hank insists he had no way of knowing Brian was gay before hiring him.
jokes.punchline: Artie: 'Barbara Streisand.' Hank: 'Aw. Aw, shit.' — The callback to Brian's resume (assistant to Streisand's assistant) retroactively reframes it as an obvious gay cultural signifier that Hank completely missed.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional callback structure. 'Barbara Streisand' as Artie's one-word, two-beat reply to Hank's protest is brilliant economy — he doesn't need to explain the logic. Hank's 'Aw. Aw, shit.' is the perfect delayed recognition. This joke rewards the entire setup of the hiring sequence and lands as one of the episode's funniest moments. The structure is near-perfect: Hank's escalating insistence ('Not... not... not one'), Artie's single-word demolition, Hank's self-condemnation. Justified 8.5+.

jokes.text: Do you know where I found this message slip? / Hank, I don't even... / In Larry's slot. / In Larry's slot. / Now I'm going to be wondering all the time, 'what else is waiting for me in Larry's slot?'
jokes.setup: Hank has discovered a misrouted message slip — it was put in Larry's slot instead of his.
jokes.punchline: 'What else is waiting for me in Larry's slot?' — delivered with complete obliviousness to the double meaning. Hank's fixation on 'Larry's slot' as a professional grievance while the audience hears a sexual connotation is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The double-entendre on 'slot' is functional but the joke leans on an accidental innuendo rather than crafted wordplay. The character specificity (Hank's agitation about Larry getting his message) is the stronger element.

jokes.text: I asked for aloe vera. / Uh-huh. And, uh, what did I ask for? / Aloe vera. / Yes, I asked for lanolin. I asked for lanolin.
jokes.setup: Hank is finding fault with Brian over the wrong lotion.
jokes.punchline: Brian has correctly identified 'aloe vera' as what Hank asked for. Hank insists he asked for lanolin. The circular absurdity — Brian correctly recites what Hank said, Hank says that's not what he meant — reveals Hank building a pretextual case.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the transparent bad faith of Hank's firing pretext. The audience knows he's trying to fire Brian for being gay; watching him work through the lotion argument while Brian — correctly — points out the discrepancy is good cringe.

jokes.text: Darlene was with me for six years. She never did this. / Hank, you asked for aloe vera. / See, that's the attitude that I cannot take.
jokes.setup: Brian factually points out that Hank asked for aloe vera.
jokes.punchline: Hank labels Brian's factual correction as 'the attitude' he can't tolerate. The firing logic has fully collapsed into tautology — being right is the offense.
jokes.explanation: Hank calling a factual correction 'that attitude' is a precise observation about how prejudice operates — when you're looking for a reason to fire someone, their competence itself becomes the infraction. It's both funny and sharp.

jokes.text: So this has nothing to do with me being gay, does it? / Oh, come on, mister. Come on. / So it's the aloe vera. / 'Cause I can certainly see how that would be the last straw. / You see? There it is again. There's that attitude thing again.
jokes.setup: Brian confronts Hank directly about whether his firing is due to his sexuality.
jokes.punchline: Brian's 'I can certainly see how that would be the last straw' — devastating deadpan sarcasm about the aloe vera — and Hank's response labeling the sarcasm as 'that attitude' is a perfect cringe loop.
jokes.explanation: Brian's sarcasm is perfectly measured — 'I can certainly see how that would be the last straw' is the funniest line Brian gets in the episode. The cringe comedy works because Brian is clearly the smarter, more dignified person in this exchange, and Hank is blissfully unable to recognize that. Hank then labels this obvious wit as 'attitude.' Strong structure and character integration.

jokes.text: I am a supporter of the gay community. I wore a red ribbon to the Emmys. I have been to several Elton John concerts. / What does that mean? / Elton John... is a gay.
jokes.setup: Hank is defending himself against the accusation that he's firing Brian for being gay.
jokes.punchline: 'Elton John... is a gay.' — The callback to the earlier 'a gay' construction, now applied to Elton John as Hank's evidence of gay-community support. The logic is completely circular. The pause before 'is a gay' suggests Hank considers this a significant revelation.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest lines. 'Elton John... is a gay' — delivered as if this is information Brian might not have — is perfect Hank Kingsley. The logic (I went to his concerts, therefore I support you) is absurdly flawed but stated with complete confidence. The callback to 'a gay' as a grammatical construction confirms this is Hank's consistent vocabulary for gayness, not a slip. High quotability because the line is absurd enough to work completely out of context.

jokes.text: Is my hair too big? What is it? I mean, my God, look at my hair. / Does my ass look any fatter in these pants or what? I mean, look at my ass. I'm touching my ass.
jokes.setup: In the background or nearby, Larry is apparently having another body-anxiety moment.
jokes.punchline: Larry asking about his ass — 'I'm touching my ass' — is a direct callback to his impression of Carvey doing him: 'Does my ass look fat? Does my ass look fat?' Larry is now performing his own impression of himself.
jokes.explanation: This is a structural high point. Larry accused Carvey of having him walk around asking 'does my ass look fat?' as a caricature. Now Larry is doing exactly that, including the physical gesture ('I'm touching my ass'). The recursion — the impression IS the reality — is the show's thesis on celebrity self-delusion. 'I'm touching my ass' as a matter-of-fact statement is also funny in isolation.

jokes.text: Um, I'm going to go get your fruit.
jokes.setup: Larry is in the background having another self-examination spiral (ass, hair). Brian is present and observing.
jokes.punchline: Brian's dignified exit — 'I'm going to go get your fruit' — in the face of Larry's bizarre behavior is the reaction beat. It's the perfect professional non-response: acknowledge nothing, perform duty, exit.
jokes.explanation: Economy is near-maximum — eight words do everything. The joke is in what Brian does NOT say. This is a reaction beat delivered through an action: I saw nothing, I will now get fruit. Perfect straight-man behavior in an insane environment.

jokes.text: The teeth are the best part.
jokes.setup: The conversation about the impression has ended with Larry apparently okay with it. Then, after a beat, Larry says this.
jokes.punchline: After several minutes of Larry trying to get Carvey to drop the teeth, he now — alone, post-conversation — volunteers that 'the teeth are the best part.' The reversal is perfect: he was negotiating the teeth out, now he endorses them. It reveals that the whole conversation was Larry managing his image, not his actual feelings.
jokes.explanation: Five words that do extraordinary work. The entire episode's impression subplot — Larry trying to protect his image while pretending he's fine with it — collapses into this five-word confession of genuine appreciation that he can only express when alone (or to someone he considers safe). The economy is flawless: nothing could be cut. The character integration is exceptional — only Larry would conduct a whole political negotiation around something he actually likes. This is the episode's strongest single-line joke.

jokes.text: Well, what? Is he going to do it? / Well, last time I saw him, he was still in his Larry makeup.
jokes.setup: Backstage, people are wondering if Carvey will actually do the impression.
jokes.punchline: 'He was still in his Larry makeup' — the fact that Carvey has gone to the trouble of getting into Larry makeup is the implicit joke. Whether he uses it or not, the preparation is excessive and funny.
jokes.explanation: Functional scene-transition joke. Sets up the on-air segment without being particularly funny on its own.

jokes.text: I just want you to remember there was only one Elvis. Look how many people imitated him. / Elvis is also fat. He has a big, fat ass. / Oh, well wear a cape and a big belt, and nobody will notice your ass.
jokes.setup: Artie is philosophizing about imitation vs. the original before the show goes live.
jokes.punchline: The Elvis-imitation wisdom pivots to an ass joke — 'Elvis is also fat. He has a big, fat ass' — which Artie then converts into actual advice: wear a cape and a belt. The cascade from philosophy to practical buttock-concealment tips is very Artie.
jokes.explanation: Good Artie beat. The swerve from grand imitation philosophy to practical ass-hiding advice is funny because of the character — Artie occupies both the poetic and the deeply mundane simultaneously.

jokes.text: Well, you look great. That's a beautiful suit. / Thank you. It's Versace. Yeah, baby, you like that? / Hey, you seem to touch yourself when you say it? / What? Touched yourself. / You said Versace, and you touched yourself. / I touched myself on the leg. / Why does yourself have to mean penis? / Good night.
jokes.setup: The on-air interview begins. Larry compliments Carvey's suit. Carvey names the brand while touching himself.
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately notes Carvey 'touched himself' when he said Versace. Carvey: 'I touched myself on the leg.' Larry: 'Why does yourself have to mean penis?' — a live television escalation that ends with Carvey pretending to end the interview. The absurd semantic argument about 'yourself' on live TV is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Why does yourself have to mean penis?' is a genuinely excellent line — it's absurd, it escalates a nothing conversation into a semantic argument about body parts on live TV, and it's completely character-consistent (Larry and Carvey as two comics who can't stop riffing even in ostensibly professional contexts). The mock-ending 'Good night' from Carvey as a callback to every awkward interview bailout is perfect timing.

jokes.text: And around 1:00 on TNT, I mean, you can watch Flipper, which is a good show 'cause that's a smart fish. I swear to God. I wish I had him in my cabinet. If there's dynamite in an underwater mine, Flipper will tell you five times out of seven.
jokes.setup: Clinton (Carvey) is describing his lazy day of television watching.
jokes.punchline: 'Flipper will tell you five times out of seven' — the specific failure rate of the dolphin's intelligence ('five out of seven' rather than all the time) is the absurdist punchline. Clinton wanting Flipper in his cabinet is the escalating absurdity.
jokes.explanation: 'Five times out of seven' is a specific comedic choice — the unreliability of Flipper's intelligence is funnier than if he said 'every time.' It's a small structural choice that reveals good joke construction. The 'cabinet' pun (government cabinet / dolphin's home?) may or may not be intentional. Slightly better than average stand-up material.

jokes.text: People say I flip-flop, and I don't. But then again, I do.
jokes.setup: Clinton (Carvey) is defending his reputation while discussing Flipper.
jokes.punchline: 'Flip-flop' as a political attack, followed immediately by confirming it: 'But then again, I do.' The structure is perfect — denial, reversal, casual self-incrimination delivered straight.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the stand-up/performance segment. 'People say I flip-flop, and I don't. But then again, I do.' is a twelve-word perfect construction. The structure (assertion, immediate reversal) is comedy 101 executed with exceptional economy. The flip-flop/Flipper double meaning (or proximity) adds a layer. Highly quotable as a standalone observation. Justifiably scores 8+ on structure and economy. Marked is_standup true as this is Carvey performing on the in-show talk show.

jokes.text: The Grumpy Old Man bit: 'In my day, we didn't have safety belts to restrain you. If you hit something and stopped suddenly, you knew where you were going... straight through the windshield. Splat. You were dead, and you loved it. Whoopee. I'm a mass of bleeding bones in a highway, and I love it.'
jokes.setup: Carvey transitions to the Grumpy Old Man character — a classic SNL character who celebrates the dangers and hardships of the past.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm a mass of bleeding bones in a highway, and I love it.' The joke is that the Grumpy Old Man finds joy in physical catastrophe — his nostalgia is for the era before safety regulations, when you could die and apparently enjoy it. The specificity of 'mass of bleeding bones' is the peak of the absurdism.
jokes.explanation: Classic Carvey character work. The Grumpy Old Man's inversion of nostalgia (celebrating harm) is a strong comedic premise. 'Mass of bleeding bones in a highway, and I love it' has good absurdist escalation. Marked is_standup true — performance on the in-show talk show.

jokes.text: In my day, we didn't have flame-retardant sleepwear. If you went to bed smoking, you woke up engulfed in flames. Whoopidy-doo, I'm on fire, and I love it. I'm a bleeding, flaming corpse, and God, I love it so. As God as my witness, I'm in heaven as I flame up in a bleeding kind of way.
jokes.setup: The Grumpy Old Man continues, now addressing flame-retardant sleepwear.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'I'm on fire' to 'bleeding, flaming corpse' to 'in heaven as I flame up in a bleeding kind of way' — each description adding new suffering that the character still enthusiastically endorses.
jokes.explanation: Strong continuation of the Grumpy Old Man bit. 'Whoopidy-doo' is a good character-specific expression. The 'bleeding kind of way' qualifier at the end has a nice absurdist rhythm. Slightly less impactful than the first beat (diminishing returns on the formula).

jokes.text: Why didn't you do the impression? / Well... I was shocked. I thought you were going to do the impression of me. / No, I could tell that bothered you. / Oh, no, no, no, I loved it.
jokes.setup: Post-show, Larry confronts Carvey about not doing the Larry Sanders impression during the interview.
jokes.punchline: Larry is angry Carvey didn't do it. Carvey says he could tell it bothered Larry. Larry immediately denies this: 'Oh, no, no, no, I loved it.' The entire episode's thesis — Larry cannot admit what he actually feels — collapses into one exchange.
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of the impression subplot. Larry told Artie to let Carvey do it so he wouldn't look like he couldn't laugh at himself. Carvey read Larry correctly and didn't do it. Now Larry, who wanted to protect the image of someone who CAN laugh at himself, is angry that the impression didn't happen — which means he DOES have to laugh at himself. And when confronted, he immediately lies. The circular cringe is perfectly constructed and earns its high score as the emotional and comedic peak of the A-plot.

jokes.text: The only problem was, you know, I was under the impression that I was supposed to do it, and it was a bit of a hassle getting the wig and the teeth. It was expensive. I'm sorry. / That's all right. You'll have the money back at the poker game tonight. / I can't make the poker game. My son's got an ear infection.
jokes.setup: Carvey explains the expense of preparing the impression (wig, teeth). Larry offers to make it up at poker.
jokes.punchline: Carvey immediately drops out of the poker game due to his son's ear infection. The deflation is funny — Larry's magnanimous offer is immediately made moot. Also, 'ear infection' as the mundane parental reality that overrides all showbiz plans is a funny detail.
jokes.explanation: Good beat. The sudden domesticity (ear infection) cutting through the show-business drama is a classic Larry Sanders Show structural joke — real life intruding on the theatrical.

jokes.text: You love the poker games. You're mad, aren't you? / No, no, no, he has an ear infection. I'm not mad. / You're mad because you think I didn't let you do the impression. / No. / Let it out. You're holding your anger in. / This is weird. That's crazy. I'm not mad. / Just tell me. Get it out. / Why should I be mad? / I have many arrows in my comedic arsenal, Larry. Let's put the Larry Sanders arrow back in the sheath and pull out the Jimmy Stewart arrow. / Bing. / Bull's-eye! / There's your anger. You're an asshole.
jokes.setup: Larry pushes Carvey to admit he's angry about not doing the impression. Carvey denies it. Larry keeps pushing.
jokes.punchline: 'I have many arrows in my comedic arsenal, Larry' — Carvey's absurd metaphor for impression-switching, followed by 'Bing. Bull's-eye! There's your anger. You're an asshole.' The 'Bing' / 'Bull's-eye' / 'You're an asshole' escalation is perfectly structured — it goes from archery metaphor to confirmation to devastating epithet in three beats.
jokes.explanation: Excellent scene. 'Many arrows in my comedic arsenal' is a wonderfully pretentious metaphor for impression repertoire. The escalation to 'There's your anger. You're an asshole.' works because it's both sudden and correct — Carvey has maneuvered Larry into revealing his anger through Larry's attempt to diagnose Carvey's anger. The inversion is elegant. Highly quotable, especially 'There's your anger. You're an asshole.' as a standalone.

jokes.text: What's really pissing me off is that your staff said come out and do Larry Sanders. He'll love it. Then I get out here. You're obviously saying, 'don't do it,' which you wouldn't tell me. Now you're saying, 'why didn't you do it?' And that does piss me off. Other than that... I love you. Okay.
jokes.setup: Carvey finally tells the truth about why he's frustrated — the mixed signals from Larry's staff vs. Larry.
jokes.punchline: 'Other than that... I love you. Okay.' — Carvey lands his legitimate grievance and then immediately deflates it with an affectionate tag. The 'other than that' construction (minimizing everything he just said) and the abrupt 'I love you. Okay.' as a peace offering is funny and real.
jokes.explanation: The 'Other than that... I love you. Okay.' is a distinctly Carvey-like way to end a rant — he can't sustain anger, so he deflates it with warmth. It's character-specific to the real Dana Carvey persona the show is capturing. Good economy.

jokes.text: I don't fucking believe Larry. What do you mean? / Well, he's so vain. He won't let Carvey do that great impression of him. / I don't blame him. If I was Larry, I'd take that little Dana Carvey and I'd dry-shave him with a flicker. / What are you talking about?
jokes.setup: Backstage, the crew is debating whether Larry was right to prevent the impression.
jokes.punchline: 'I'd dry-shave him with a flicker' — Artie's defense of Larry escalates immediately to physical violence, using a specific and obscure implement ('flicker'). Phil's genuine confusion ('What are you talking about?') is the reaction beat.
jokes.explanation: Classic Artie. 'Dry-shave him with a flicker' is the kind of specific, vaguely archaic threat that only Artie would produce. The callback to Artie's pattern of extreme loyalty-violence (see: 'chinless little cocksuckers') makes it a running character joke. Phil's genuine confusion about what a flicker is adds the reaction beat that sells it.

jokes.text: Just because Larry has his own show doesn't mean he's not a human being. How would you feel, Phil, if one of your friends wanted to make you look like a sniveling, annoying fool on national television?
jokes.setup: Artie defends Larry against the charge of vanity.
jokes.punchline: Artie describes the impression as making Larry 'look like a sniveling, annoying fool' — which is also a fairly accurate description of Larry Sanders generally. The defense inadvertently confirms what it's trying to deny.
jokes.explanation: Good ironic beat. Artie's defense of Larry using language that confirms the unflattering impression is accurate is a classic dramatic irony move.

jokes.text: Dana Carvey obviously hurt him with that impression. / He did. Thank you. / Very refreshing.
jokes.setup: Artie defends Larry backstage. Larry apparently overhears.
jokes.punchline: 'He did. Thank you. Very refreshing.' — Larry grateful for Artie's validation, calling it 'refreshing' as if he's been parched for someone to confirm his feelings. The word 'refreshing' for emotional validation is funny and Larry-specific.
jokes.explanation: Good small beat. 'Very refreshing' as a descriptor for emotional agreement is specific and funny. Larry treating Artie's backstage defense as a gift he's been waiting for is character comedy.

jokes.text: Larry, I think you were absolutely right in not letting Carvey do that impression of you. / Really? Oh, absolutely. / He's supposed to be a friend of yours. He should know better. He should know that something like that would hurt your feelings. That's what I thought. / I think you should dry-shave that little fucker with a flicker.
jokes.setup: Artie validates Larry's feelings about the impression.
jokes.punchline: 'I think you should dry-shave that little fucker with a flicker.' — The callback to Artie's earlier threat, now deployed as sincere advice directly to Larry. Larry's 'Right, that's exactly right. What's a flicker?' admits he doesn't know either.
jokes.explanation: The callback lands because Larry's 'What's a flicker?' reveals that neither Larry nor Artie knows what a flicker is — Artie has been deploying this threat without a referent. The shared ignorance of the implement of violence is very funny. The running gag pays off completely.

jokes.text: Where do you think you're going, Mr. Hank Kingsley's permanent assistant? / I thought you were uncomfortable with me being gay. / I am, but where else am I going to find a personal assistant who'll tell me when Larry is hurt?
jokes.setup: Brian is apparently leaving after being fired. Hank stops him.
jokes.punchline: Hank's reason for rehiring Brian — 'where else am I going to find a personal assistant who'll tell me when Larry is hurt?' — is entirely self-serving and uses Brian's human insight as a professional commodity. Hank's 'I am' (still uncomfortable with the gay thing) delivered with total honesty before the pivot is very Hank.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. Hank's honesty ('I am [uncomfortable]') paired with his entirely practical reason for keeping Brian anyway is deeply Hank — he's homophobic but pragmatic, and his pragmatism wins. 'Where else am I going to find a personal assistant who'll tell me when Larry is hurt?' is both funny and a surprisingly tender line about Hank's deep care for Larry, expressed through pure utility.

jokes.text: You ordered aloe vera. / Yes, I did. I'm sorry. Forgive me.
jokes.setup: Brian (now rehired) produces the lotion again. Hank has been forced to admit he asked for aloe vera.
jokes.punchline: Hank's 'Yes, I did. I'm sorry. Forgive me.' — a full capitulation on the pretextual reason he tried to fire Brian. The apology is enormous in proportion to the offense. Hank has lost the argument, and he knows it.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the aloe vera pretense. Hank's formal, exaggerated apology ('Forgive me') over a lotion while simultaneously rehiring Brian is funny in its disproportion. The entire sequence of fake reasons has collapsed into this admission.

jokes.text: And Doug Llewelyn didn't call, did he? / Doug Llewelyn's a faggot. / Sorry.
jokes.setup: Hank asks about a missed call from Doug Llewelyn (the People's Court reporter).
jokes.punchline: Brian, who has just been through a whole episode of being fired for being gay, casually drops a homophobic slur about Llewelyn — then immediately says 'Sorry.' The irony of a gay man using that slur, immediately caught by his own self-correction, is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent button joke. The irony is sharp and dark — Brian, who was nearly fired for being gay, uses an anti-gay slur within sixty seconds of being reinstated. His immediate 'Sorry' suggests habitual self-correction rather than genuine reconsideration. The joke refuses to sentimentalize the resolution; Brian is flawed, complicated, and kind of brilliant. Economy is near-perfect: three words plus one word reply do everything.

jokes.text: I am going to kick their asses. / He seems really angry. / Aw, fuck Dana. We don't need him. / Well, maybe you're right. / You feeling lucky tonight, my boy? / Well, I got a boner. / Whoa, we're all in trouble.
jokes.setup: The gang prepares for poker. Hank is confident. Artie and Larry exchange pleasantries.
jokes.punchline: Larry: 'You feeling lucky tonight, my boy?' Larry: 'Well, I got a boner.' The abrupt non sequitur (erection as poker confidence indicator), followed by Artie's 'Whoa, we're all in trouble' — accepting the logic — is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Well, I got a boner' as a poker confidence statement — and Artie accepting this as a legitimate measure of luck ('We're all in trouble') — is funny and fast. The exchange captures the easy locker-room camaraderie between the three core characters.

jokes.text: Larry, Dana Carvey just called from his car, and he's coming to the poker game. / Hey, now we don't need Hank.
jokes.setup: Carvey, who bailed on poker earlier due to his son's ear infection, now calls to say he's coming after all.
jokes.punchline: 'Hey, now we don't need Hank.' — The instant substitution of Hank with Carvey, delivered casually, is the episode's closing joke. Hank's inclusion in the poker game was itself a consolation prize after the Darlene devastation; now he's immediately expendable.
jokes.explanation: Perfect closing joke. Hank was invited to poker specifically because he needed cheering up after Darlene's letter. The instant 'we don't need Hank' when Carvey calls is the episode's final word on how Hollywood friendships work — replaceable, transactional, and slightly cruel. The delivery presumably comes right as Hank is riding the high of his poker confidence ('I got a boner'). Economical, earned, and structurally satisfying as an episode closer.

tmdb_overview: When Darlene quits while on vacation, Hank hires the temp who was filling in for her. Larry's reluctant to tell Dana Carvey he doesn't like Carvey's Larry Sanders impersonation.
